source_note: Criterion definitions follow the CVS protocol; concise prompt wording is informed by the public CVS-AdaptNet prompt interface.

positive: The gallbladder is attached only to two tubular structures: the cystic duct and the cystic artery.
Only the cystic duct and cystic artery remain visibly connected to the gallbladder.
Exactly two tubular structures enter the gallbladder, corresponding to the cystic duct and cystic artery.
negative: The cystic duct and cystic artery are not both clearly identified as the only structures attached to the gallbladder.
More than two structures or unclear tissue connections remain attached to the gallbladder.
The two tubular structures entering the gallbladder cannot yet be distinguished with confidence.

positive: The lower gallbladder is separated from the liver bed and the cystic plate is clearly exposed.
Dissection of the lower gallbladder from the liver reveals the cystic plate.
The lower third of the gallbladder has been lifted from the liver bed with the cystic plate visible.
negative: The lower gallbladder remains attached to the liver bed and the cystic plate is not clearly exposed.
Residual tissue obscures separation of the lower gallbladder from the liver and hides the cystic plate.
The cystic plate is absent or incompletely visible because liver-bed dissection is insufficient.

positive: The hepatocystic triangle is fully cleared of fat and fibrous connective tissue.
Fat and connective tissue have been removed from the hepatocystic triangle to provide an unobstructed view.
The Calot triangle is completely dissected and its anatomy is clearly visible.
negative: Fat or fibrous connective tissue still obscures the hepatocystic triangle.
The Calot triangle is not fully dissected and its anatomy remains unclear.
Residual tissue prevents an unobstructed view through the hepatocystic triangle.
